newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily coffee report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

The November contract in London closed below nearby $1,500 support at $1,495, after origin and speculator selling finally managed to outstrip industry purchases earlier in the session. All other traded positions were also weaker. Traders cited Far East selling, including Indonesia, as being responsible for the weakness.

In New York, arabica futures closed mixed with front month December losing 80 points to close at 103.60 cents/lb. March ended 35 points easier at 100.60 cents/lb. The back months added 5 to 35 points. Even though spreads on coffees for forward delivery inched lower as roasters anticipated the flow of new-crop beans from Central and South America in the coming months, recent inventory figures show spot supplies are still hard to come by.

The Green Coffee Association reported earlier this week that US warehouse stocks of green coffee declined by 93,000 60-kg bags in August, to 1.816 million bags, the lowest level in seven years. Meanwhile the CSCE's certified stock figures were unchanged on the week at 42,677 60-kg bags.

COSTA RICA - Losses caused by Hurricane Cesar are less than had been originally feared, the executive director of the Costa Rica Coffee Institute (ICAFE), Guillermo Canet, told Reuters. Losses registered to date total 111,000 bags, while originally the loss was put at 460,000 bags.

Total production in 1996/97 (October/September) is now estimated to reach 2.377 million 60-kg bags down from 2.606 million bags produced the previous year. Hurricane Cesar smashed into Costa Rica a month ago and caused widespread damage both to coffee beans and infrastructure.
Canet said the government is working flat out to repair roads and bridges in the regions worst affected, including the coffee growing zones of Los Santos, Perez Zeledon and Coto Brus.

INDIA - Industry sources fear that domestic prices will rise following the decision to introduce a 100 per cent free-sale quota. It was said this decision will encourage more growers to export available coffee, capturing lucrative overseas markets at the cost of the domestic consumer.

Ramesh Rajah, president of the Coffee Exporters Association, said growers would be keen to hold back their produce, putting pressure on roasters. Growers said unseasonal rains had reduced India's coffee output prospects in 1995/96 (October/September) to less than 3.3 million 60-kg bags, down from earlier forecasts of 3.9 million bags.

ITALY - Italy imported 423,869 bags of coffee in April 1996, 21 per cent more than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1996 up to 1.966 million bags, 8.6 per cent more than was imported the same period in 1995. Total imports in calendar year 1995 dropped by 1.6 per cent to 5.387 million bags.

Major suppliers of green coffee in January/April 1996 were Ivory Coast (117,700 vs 115,600 bags), Uganda (114,500 vs 90,000 bags), Zaire (193,500 vs 258,800 bags), Brazil (442,000 vs 510,200 bags), Colombia (161,300 vs 101,600 bags) and India (161,300 vs 139,100 bags).

The country exported 257,600 bags of coffee in January/April 1996, 24 per cent more than was exported the same period in 1995. Total exports in calendar year 1995 rose by 5.2 per cent to 738,900 bags.
